'GSAERU utilizes a graph autoencoder to learn node representations.'"}], "reader_texts": ["With the increasing stealth and severity of cyberattacks, the demand for advanced persistent threat (APT) detection systems that deeply understand complex system behaviors has grown substantially. However, existing provenance-based methods often struggle to balance prediction accuracy with inference latency across distributed, resource-constrained environments. To address this, we propose CE-GTC , a collaborative intelligence framework that synergizes large and small models across the cloud-edge continuum. Specifically, the system constructs provenance graphs to capture causal system interactions. In the cloud, a heavy Graph Transformer (the large model) performs computationally intensive representation learning—utilizing edge-feature injection and self-supervised objectives—to extract discriminative embeddings and compact normal behavior profiles. Meanwhile, edge devices host a lightweight clustering detector (the small model) for real-time, privacy-aware anomaly detection via Inverse Document Frequency (IDF)-weighted hybrid distance computation against multi-cluster centers. Experimental evaluations on the Unicorn Wget and StreamSpot datasets demonstrate that CE-GTC achieves superior performance, including an F1-score up to 0.974 and response latency under one second. This highlights the effectiveness of large-small model synergy for scalable, secure, and intelligent APT detection.", "Graph Continual Learning aims to enable models to acquire knowledge from sequentially arriving graph tasks while preserving performance on previously learned tasks. However, training on new tasks can overwrite learned representations and parameters, leading to catastrophic forgetting. Existing methods mainly mitigate forgetting through experience replay, regularization constraints, or parameter isolation, but they often lack an explicit mechanism for modeling selective forgetting. To address this issue, we propose Task-Correlation-Guided Memory Regulation (TCMR), which uses learnable task correlation as a unified control signal to jointly guide memory retention, replacement, and replay. In addition, TCMR introduces a correlation-weighted parameter consolidation mechanism to enable differentiated knowledge preservation and updating. Specifically, historical parameter anchors are protected according to task relevance, which helps prevent highly correlated old-task knowledge from being overwritten during long task sequences. Experiments under node-level continual learning with both task-incremental learning (Task-IL) and class-incremental learning (Class-IL) settings show that the proposed method effectively alleviates catastrophic forgetting and achieves competitive performance in most experimental settings.", "The mechanism distinguishing visual subitizing (small n ) from estimation (large n ) is unknown. We propose a theoretical mechanism based on the dynamical stability of an On-Centre Off-Surround (OCOS) recurrent neural network. A linear stability analysis of the model reveals that the spectrum of modal decay rates ( $$\\lambda _k$$ λ k ) is parametrically controlled by numerosity ( n ) and inhibition ( $$\\beta $$ β ). We derive that for small n , the system is highly stable, causing all noise-driven fluctuations to decay rapidly. As n increases, the network is tuned towards a critical boundary. This “critical slowing down” creates a dense spectrum of slow modes, which theoretically generates persistent, long-range temporal correlations (LRTCs). The model thus predicts that subitizing should be a dynamically memoryless (white noise) process, while estimation should exhibit persistent LRTCs (pink noise). To evaluate this prediction, we re-analyzed reaction time (RT) series from a continuous enumeration task. The empirical results aligned with our theoretical derivation: Subitizing RTs were effectively uncorrelated ( $$\\alpha _{\\text {DFA}}= 0.498 \\pm 0.083$$ α DFA = 0.498 ± 0.083 ), matching the prediction for a stable system. In contrast, estimation RTs exhibited a mean exponent characteristic of dynamical persistence ( $$\\alpha _{\\text {DFA}}= 0.674 \\pm 0.087$$ α DFA = 0.674 ± 0.087 ). Although high inter-subject variability limited the statistical significance of this contrast, the dynamical persistence in the estimation regime was behaviorally relevant: subjects with higher $$\\alpha _{\\text {DFA}}$$ α DFA exhibited a larger RT switch cost when moving from estimation to subitizing ( $$r \\approx 0.41$$ r ≈ 0.41 ). We conclude that the subitizing-estimation divide may reflect a fundamental transition in the dynamical stability of the underlying neural system.", "In the recent era, social network is a powerful technology to express our views and build the new friendship. But, due to easy process of creating the account in social network, there are number of fake users in the network. Due to the fake users, the fraudulent messages are spread in the network. In this paper, the clustering-based approach is proposed for identifying the fake user in the unattributed static social network. Here, the twitter data set is used to detect the fake users in it. The dataset is represented in graph based on its connections. The nodes in graph are grouped together to form a community using dragon fly clustering. The nodes which are having high Jaccard index are determined as outlier node in the community-based data. Because, this node act as a bridge between the community and it does not belong to any particular community. The optimal feature is detected using Dragon Fly – Neural Network (DF-NN) algorithm by reducing the error rate of the classifier to detect the fake nodes. The proposed method is evaluated using Accuracy and True positive rate with the existing PCA-SVM classification method.", "Temporal graphs are a variety of structured data that have been particularly studied recently. In this paper, we focus on classification of temporal graphs. Previous works have shown that such task can be tackled by first transforming temporal graphs to static ones using ad-hoc algorithms, before the classification step. However, resulting static graphs might be of huge size. Transitive reduction can be used to reduce the size and redundancy of such graphs, but with a high complexity time. In this paper, we propose a fully dynamic algorithm that transforms temporal graphs into static ones while applying exact transitive reduction at the same time. This algorithm has a much reduced complexity than doing both steps separately, while producing exactly the same output graphs. We show in the experimental section that similar accuracy is achieved for a lower computational time.", "AI-based song generation is rapidly advancing, using deep learning to create new and creative music. AI–generated music can create personalized soundtracks for different users and help artists come up with new musical ideas. In recent times, Large Language Models(LLMs) and transformer–based frameworks, music generated by these models sounds more natural, well–structured, and more flexible than before. This paper reviews all of the latest AI models used in music generation, including transformer models such as MusicGen and hybrid approaches that combine different neural network types . This study compares the datasets and tools used in research, including the MusicGen pre–training data set, the Million Piano-roll Dataset and other data sets built for specific styles or genres. Observations show that transformers are great for making well-structured music, while GANs are better at adding creativity and variation. LLMs are the most powerful and adaptable, but the field still needs better evaluation methods and more diverse data. To create AI music generation better, work should focus on common evaluation standards, global music data and smartly combined AI models.", "Temporal networks have gained significant prominence in the past decade for modelling dynamic interactions within complex systems. A key challenge in this domain is Temporal Link Prediction (TLP), which aims to forecast future connections by analysing historical network structures across a range of applications. While existing surveys have addressed specific aspects of TLP, they typically lack a comprehensive framework that distinguishes between representation and inference methods, the two key ingredients of TLP. This survey bridges this gap by introducing a novel taxonomy that explicitly examines representation and inference in existing methods, providing a novel classification of approaches for TLP. We analyse how different representation techniques capture temporal and structural dynamics, examining their compatibility with various inference methods for link prediction tasks. Our taxonomy not only clarifies the methodological landscape but also reveals promising unexplored combinations of existing techniques. This taxonomy provides a systematic foundation for tackling emerging challenges in TLP, including model explainability and scalable architectures for complex temporal networks.", "Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a class of deep learning models that have demonstrated significant potential in various classification tasks, including image recognition and the prediction of labels for nodes and edges. Unlike traditional neural networks that operate on Euclidean data such as images or sequences, GNNs are specifically designed to handle non-Euclidean data, i.e. data represented as graphs, where relationships between entities are irregular and complex. These graphs may include rich node and edge attributes, making GNNs particularly suitable for domains such as social networks, molecular structures, and recommendation systems. Several GNN variants have been developed, including GCN, Cluster-GCN, GraphSAGE, and FastGCN. Despite their advantages, GNNs often require substantial memory, primarily due to the large adjacency matrices involved, which become computationally expensive for large-scale graphs. They also tend to have long training times. In this work, we propose a novel graph partitioning technique aimed at reducing the effective size of the graph while maintaining a high predictive F1-score. Furthermore, we integrate this partitioning approach with layer-wise training to enhance computational efficiency.", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", ""], "finish_schema": {"$defs": {"EvidenceCardDraft": {"additionalProperties": false, "description": "One model-authored semantic assessment to be bound by the runtime.", "properties": {"main_contribution": {"minLength": 1, "title": "Main Contribution", "type": "string"}, "overlaps": {"items": {"minLength": 1, "type": "string"}, "title": "Overlaps", "type": "array"}, "differences": {"items": {"minLength": 1, "type": "string"}, "title": "Differences", "type": "array"}, "quotes": {"items": {"$ref": "#/$defs/EvidenceQuoteDraft"}, "minItems": 1, "title": "Quotes", "type": "array"}, "possible_baseline": {"default": false, "title": "Possible Baseline", "type": "boolean"}, "relevance": {"maximum": 1.0, "minimum": 0.0, "title": "Relevance", "type": "number"}, "confidence": {"maximum": 1.0, "minimum": 0.0, "title": "Confidence", "type": "number"}}, "required": ["main_contribution", "quotes", "relevance", "confidence"], "title": "EvidenceCardDraft", "type": "object"}, "EvidenceQuoteDraft": {"additionalProperties": false, "description": "A semantic quote selection without model-supplied provenance handles.", "properties": {"quote": {"minLength": 1, "title": "Quote", "type": "string"}, "interpretation": {"minLength": 1, "title": "Interpretation", "type": "string"}, "confidence": {"maximum": 1.0, "minimum": 0.0, "title": "Confidence", "type": "number"}}, "required": ["quote", "interpretation", "confidence"], "title": "EvidenceQuoteDraft", "type": "object"}}, "additionalProperties": false, "properties": {"cards": {"items": {"$ref": "#/$defs/EvidenceCardDraft"}, "title": "Cards", "type": "array"}, "no_evidence_reason": {"anyOf": [{"minLength": 1, "type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}], "default": null, "title": "No Evidence Reason"}}, "title": "ResearchFinishDraft", "type": "object"}}
